# Wireshark Traffic Analysis — Home Network

**Project:** Real-World Cyber Security Projects — Project 2 (Traffic Analysis with Wireshark)
**Analyst:** Zain Ul Abdin — Zain Tech Automation Solutions
**Date:** 31 October 2026
**Environment:** Personal home lab only — Kali Linux VM on my own home network. All traffic analysed was generated by my own virtual machine.

---

## 1. Objective

Capture live traffic from my own machine and learn to read it: identify the protocols involved when a computer uses a network, separate background noise from real activity, and observe the difference between encrypted and unencrypted communication.

## 2. Setup & Tools

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Tool | Wireshark 4.6.9 |
| Machine | Kali Linux 2026.3 (VirtualBox VM, Bridged Adapter) |
| Capture interface | `eth0` |
| VM address | 192.168.1.20 |
| Gateway / DNS server | 192.168.1.1 (home fiber router) |
| Test sites | example.org, neverssl.com (deliberately plain-HTTP test site) |

## 3. Method

Traffic was captured on `eth0` while generating controlled activity from the VM's own browser, then isolated with display filters:

- `dns` — name-resolution traffic only
- `http` — plain-HTTP web traffic only
- `arp` — local address-resolution traffic
- `tcp.port == 80` — one complete TCP conversation
- `ip.addr == 192.168.1.1` — everything to/from the router only

## 4. Findings

### 4.1 DNS — asking for the address (before anything else)
- My VM asked the router (UDP destination port 53): `Standard query 0xe3b1 A example.org` — packet 284.
- The router answered with the **same transaction ID**: `Standard query response 0xe3b1 A example.org` — packet 289. Query/response pairs are matched by this ID.
- The browser asked for both `A` (IPv4) and `AAAA` (IPv6) records.
- Background traffic was identified as normal system noise, not user activity: Firefox checks `detectportal.firefox.com` and `ipv4only.arpa` on its own.
- **Security note:** DNS is unencrypted — the names of sites being resolved are readable in plain text in the packet bytes, visible to anyone who can capture traffic on the network path.
- Queries and responses were separated using `dns.flags.response == 0` (queries only) and `== 1` (responses only).

### 4.2 HTTP — the actual conversation, fully readable
- Firefox's connectivity check was captured end-to-end: `GET /success.txt?ipv4 HTTP/1.1` → `HTTP/1.1 200 OK (text/plain)`.
- The deliberately unencrypted site neverssl.com was captured in full: `GET /` → `200 OK (text/html)`, a `301 Moved Permanently` redirect for its /online page, and even its `favicon.ico` image (PNG) — every part readable in plain text, including request headers (e.g. the browser's User-Agent string).
- **Security note:** on plain HTTP there is no protection at all — anything sent (a page request today, a password on a weaker site) crosses the network readable by whoever can capture it.

### 4.3 TCP — how a reliable conversation is opened and closed
Using `tcp.port == 80`, one full connection lifecycle was read:
- **Handshake (3 steps):** `[SYN]` (client → server) → `[SYN, ACK]` (server) → `[ACK]` (client). Only after these three steps did the HTTP request go out.
- Through the conversation, `[ACK]` packets act as receipts confirming data arrived.
- The conversation ended politely with `[FIN, ACK]`.
- Port reading: server side used the well-known port **80**; my VM used a temporary **ephemeral port (54866)** created for this one conversation.

### 4.4 ARP — finding the actual machine inside the home
- My VM broadcast to the whole network: `Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.20`.
- The router replied directly: `192.168.1.1 is at 28:23:f5:c9:fe:58`.
- The capture also showed ARP probes and announcements: a device checks that its address is not already taken, then announces itself to the network.
- **Security note:** ARP has **no authentication** — a device simply believes whoever answers. This is the weakness behind ARP-spoofing attacks (to be studied hands-on in a later lab project).

### 4.5 Looking only at the router (`ip.addr == 192.168.1.1`)
- Only the DNS exchanges appeared. Reason: DNS questions **end at** the router (it is the LAN's DNS server), while web traffic only **passes through** it on the way to outside servers — it is not addressed to the router itself.

## 5. Key Distinctions Learned

| Protocol | Job | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| DNS | Turns a site name into an IP address — always the first step | Asking for the address before travelling |
| HTTP | Carries the actual content (pages, files) after the address is known | The visit/conversation itself |
| ARP | Turns an IP address into a hardware (MAC) address **inside** the local network | Finding the actual house on the street |
| TCP | Opens, tracks (receipts) and closes a reliable conversation | A registered-post conversation vs. a postcard |

- A **capture filter** decides what gets recorded; a **display filter** decides what gets shown afterwards — they are not the same box.
- Background/system traffic (browser connectivity checks, address announcements) is constant and normal; an analyst's first skill is recognising it so real events stand out.

## 6. Conclusion

Starting from a raw capture of thousands of packets, display filters reduced the noise to readable conversations. I can now follow a DNS exchange end-to-end and pair its question with its answer, read a complete unencrypted HTTP session, trace a TCP connection from handshake to teardown, and explain how devices find each other locally via ARP — and why two of these protocols (DNS, ARP) deserve a security analyst's suspicion.

## 7. Scope & Ethics

This analysis was performed in my own home lab, on my own network, on traffic generated by my own virtual machine. No third-party network or device was targeted.
